adults.title: When We Cannot Fix It
adults.big_idea: Because God loves us, He uses the hard things we cannot fix to shape us to become like Him, and the Savior does His deepest work when we invite Him in.
adults.objective: Learners will name one burden they cannot fix and choose one specific way this week to invite the Savior into it with trust instead of asking only why.
prepare: Read Sister Runia's talk, especially paragraphs 10–16 (umbrella and rock) and 36–47 (the sculpting class).
Bring a shoelace or piece of string tied in a tight knot.
Bring a slip of paper and a pencil for each person.
Draw a simple umbrella and a simple rock on the board before class.
Pray by name for class members who are carrying something heavy.

segments.name: Things we cannot fix
steps: Begin with prayer. Hand the knotted shoelace to someone near the front and ask them to work on it while you talk.

Explain that Sister Runia said she loves fixing things: knots, stains, problems. Then, thirteen years ago, her oldest son, Ryan, left for work one Monday and died a few hours later when his heart stopped. The next day was his daughter Piper's second birthday. As the family sang and Piper looked for her dad, Sister Runia realized this was something she would not be able to fix.

Give each person a slip of paper. Invite them to write, privately, one thing in their life or in the life of someone they love that they cannot fix. No one will see it. Ask them to keep it in their hand during the lesson.
questions: Without sharing what you wrote: what does it feel like to face something you cannot fix?

segments.name: Umbrella or rock
steps: Point to the umbrella on the board. Explain that Sister Runia grew up hearing true promises about blessings for keeping the commandments, so the gospel felt like a big umbrella that would keep the rain off her. She has learned from experience that we are all going to get rained on.
Read her sentence from paragraph 12 aloud (first key quote) and point to the rock.
In pairs, read Helaman 5:12. Ask each pair to find two things: what the verse says will come, and what it promises.
Invite two or three pairs to report, then discuss the questions as a class.
questions: What changes in how we pray and how we endure when we stop expecting an umbrella and start standing on the rock?
When has the Savior held you steady in a storm that did not stop?

segments.name: From why to what
steps: Explain the setting Sister Runia described: Joseph Smith in a jail cell, pleading with God for a break from his circumstance. Have someone read D&C 122:7. Note the answer she quoted: “All these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.”
Have someone read 1 Nephi 11:16–17. Ask the class what Nephi knew and what he admitted he did not know.
Read the second key quote (paragraph 14). Write on the board: Why? on the left, and on the right: I know that God loves me, so what...?
Tell the class that at Ryan's funeral Sister Runia said she did not understand why this happened, and then added: “Not understanding is not the same as not believing.”
Pair-share for three minutes on the first question below. Then read Elder Hathaway's words (aligned quote) and invite one or two to share with the class.
questions: When have you had to hold on to God's love without having an answer? What helped you keep believing?
How is starting from God's love different from starting from why?

segments.name: The Master's hand
steps: Retell the story Sister Runia shared from her brother Kent. In a college sculpting class he had to sculpt a bust of himself from clay. He could not get the eyes to look lifelike. He saw the instructor helping others but wanted the piece to be his own, so he struggled alone for quite a while before he humbled himself and asked. The instructor carved so abruptly and aggressively that it startled him, digging much deeper than Kent had. Within a few minutes the eyes came to life. Kent saw that the piece was uniquely him, and yet “a master’s hand had shaped what mine could not.”
In groups of three or four, read paragraphs 43–46 of the talk (from a phone or printout). Ask each group to choose the one sentence that speaks to them most and tell why.
Hear briefly from each group.
questions: Sister Runia said our pride gets in the way of inviting the Savior to become involved. What does that pride sound like in ordinary life?
What does an invitation to the Savior actually look like on a hard Tuesday?

segments.name: A choice right now
steps: Tell the class that the day before Ryan died he was set apart as elders quorum president and visited a neighbor whose wife and children had just left him. Ryan told him he had a big choice: he could curse God and blame Him, or turn to Him and let Him heal him.
Read Sister Runia's invitation (see invitations) and her promise: “And He can fix what feels badly broken.” Read 1 John 3:2 together as the end of the story she testified of.
Invite everyone to look at their slip of paper and write beneath it one specific way they will invite the Savior into that burden this week. Allow a full minute of silence.
Check for understanding: ask one person to say in a sentence what it means that the gospel is the rock and not the umbrella.
Bear your testimony of the Savior. Tell the class that next week you will begin by asking what they noticed when they prayed with what instead of only why.

key_quotes.text: The gospel isn’t the umbrella; it’s the solid rock we’re standing on during the storm—that “sure foundation … whereon if men build they cannot fall.”
God’s love has moved me from questions that begin with “why” to reflections that begin, “I know that God loves me, so what is supposed to be happening here?”
Not understanding is not the same as not believing.
God is shaping us into something only He knows we can become.

scriptures.use: Read in pairs during the umbrella or rock segment. Find what the verse says will come and what it promises.
One person reads aloud after you describe Joseph Smith pleading in a jail cell. Ask what the Lord gave him instead of a reprieve.
Read aloud. Ask what Nephi knew and what he admitted he did not know, then connect to Sister Runia's move from why to what.
Read together in the last segment as the promised end of the shaping: what we will see and what we will be.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Hathaway
aligned_quotes.text: This grace does not remove the pain and difficulty of affliction; it is an enabling power

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Dunn
aligned_quotes.text: Peace will come even when hoped-for outcomes do not.

invitations.text: Let’s choose Christ, who can heal the wounds of this world while carving out room for joy!

takeaways: The gospel is not an umbrella that keeps the rain off; it is the rock I stand on in the storm.
I can believe without understanding, and begin my questions from God's love.
The Savior waits for my invitation, and His hand can shape what mine cannot.
act: Each day this week, pray about the burden on your slip of paper and ask what Heavenly Father would have you learn or become, not only why it happened.
Say one honest sentence in prayer that invites the Savior in, such as: I have been trying to do this alone; please help me.
Reread paragraphs 43–47 of the talk on one quiet evening and write down where you can already see the work of His hand.
Sit with someone who is carrying something that cannot be fixed. Listen; do not try to fix it.
adapt: At home with one or two adults: skip the groups. Read paragraphs 43–46 together and take turns answering the questions; write on the slips together in silence.
Large class: do every discussion as pair-share first, then take only two comments each time so you finish.
Only 15 minutes: do the first segment, the umbrella or rock segment, and the final writing.

youth.title: Trust the One Who Designed It
youth.big_idea: Hard things do not mean God has forgotten me; He loves me, He has a plan, and He is shaping me into someone only He knows I can become.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to turn a why question into a trusting question that starts from God's love, and will choose one hard thing to invite the Savior into this week.
prepare: Read Sister Runia's talk, especially paragraphs 10–14, 25–27 and 36–46.
Bring paper and a pen for each person.
Ask the youth to have their scriptures or the Gospel Library app ready.
Draw an umbrella and a rock on the board.

segments.name: Draw without the picture
steps: As soon as youth sit down, hand out paper and pens. Say you will give instructions and they may not ask what they are drawing.

Give these steps quickly: Draw a square in the middle of the page. Put a triangle on top that touches it. Add a small rectangle at the bottom of the square. Draw a circle in a top corner of the page with short lines coming out of it.
Have them hold up their pages. Ask the question below and take two quick answers.
questions: What was it like to follow the steps without knowing what the picture would be?

segments.name: Only the instructions
steps: Tell the story honestly and gently: Sister Runia's oldest son, Ryan, died suddenly one Monday when his heart stopped. He had a wife, Cari, and four young children. At the funeral his seven-year-old son, Jaac, shared a Primary talk he and his dad had written two weeks earlier. Jaac said he loves Lego bricks and follows the instructions, and that Heavenly Father's plan is like that: if we follow it, “we can build hard things.”
Then Cari asked Jaac what he would do if he did not have the picture on the box, only the instructions. Have a youth read his answer (first key quote).
Discuss in pairs for one minute, then as a class.
questions: Why is it harder to trust a designer than to trust a picture on the box?
What helps you trust Heavenly Father when you cannot see how something will turn out?

segments.name: Umbrella or rock
steps: Ask the honest question out loud: If I keep the commandments, why do hard things still happen to me? Tell them Sister Runia asked the same thing. She grew up hearing true promises about blessings, so the gospel felt like a big umbrella to keep the rain off. Then she learned that everyone gets rained on.
Friendly race: split into two teams. Each team opens Helaman 5:12 and lists every kind of storm the verse names and the one thing it promises. First team with a complete list reads it aloud.
Read the second key quote (paragraph 12) and point to the umbrella and the rock on the board.
Discuss the questions.
questions: According to the verse, is the storm a matter of if or when? What difference does that make?
What does standing on the rock look like for someone your age during a bad week?

segments.name: Change the question
steps: Set the scene Sister Runia described: Joseph Smith in a jail cell, pleading with God for a break. Have a youth read D&C 122:7 and say what answer he received instead.
Read the third key quote (paragraph 14). Write on the board her new question: “I know that God loves me, so what is supposed to be happening here?”

In pairs, give each pair one made-up situation: you trained all summer and did not make the team; your closest friend moved away; you have prayed about something for months and nothing seems to change. Each pair writes the why question a person would ask, then rewrites it starting from God's love.
Have each pair read both versions. Ask the class which version leaves more room for God to help.
Read Elder Chigbundu's words (aligned quote). Add that Sister Runia said not understanding is not the same as not believing.
questions: Is it wrong to ask why? What did Nephi say he knew and did not know in 1 Nephi 11:17?

segments.name: Ask the Master
steps: Tell the story of Sister Runia's brother Kent. In a college sculpting class he had to sculpt a bust of himself from clay and could not get the eyes right. The instructor was helping others, but Kent wanted the piece to be his own and struggled alone until he finally humbled himself and asked. The instructor dug into the clay much further than Kent had, so abruptly that it startled him, and within minutes the eyes came to life. The piece was uniquely Kent, yet shaped by a master's hand.
Read the fourth key quote (paragraph 44): “He waits for an invitation before He can really go to work.”
Read President Chibota's words (aligned quote) and discuss the questions.
questions: Why do we wait so long to ask for help, from people and from the Savior?
Kent said the piece was still uniquely him. What does that tell you about what the Savior wants to make of you?

segments.name: Your choice this week
steps: Read Sister Runia's invitation (see invitations) and her promise that the Savior can fix what feels badly broken.
On the back of their drawing, each youth writes one hard thing in their life right now and one sentence they will pray each day this week to invite the Savior into it. This stays private.
Check for understanding: ask one youth to explain the umbrella and the rock in ten seconds.
Bear a short testimony. Tell them that next week you will ask who tried the daily sentence and what they noticed.

key_quotes.text: Yes, because you can trust the one who designed it, and it always turns out.
The gospel isn’t the umbrella; it’s the solid rock we’re standing on during the storm
God’s love has moved me from questions that begin with “why” to reflections that begin, “I know that God loves me, so what is supposed to be happening here?”
He waits for an invitation before He can really go to work.

scriptures.use: Team race: list every kind of storm the verse names and the one thing it promises to those who build on the rock.
One youth reads aloud after you describe Joseph Smith in the jail cell. Ask what answer he received instead of a break.
Read during the question segment. Ask what Nephi knew for sure and what he admitted he did not know.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Chigbundu
aligned_quotes.text: The burden we carry may not always be removed, but our backs will be built to carry the load placed upon them

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Chibota
aligned_quotes.text: He sees not only who we are but who we can become.

invitations.text: Let’s choose Christ, who can heal the wounds of this world while carving out room for joy!

takeaways: The gospel is the rock under my feet, not an umbrella over my head.
I can start my hardest questions with what I know: God loves me.
The Savior waits for me to invite Him, and I can trust the One who designed the plan.
act: Pray your one sentence every day this week, inviting the Savior into the hard thing you wrote down.
The next time something goes wrong, stop and rewrite your why question so it begins from God's love.
Put Jaac's answer about trusting the designer on your lock screen or mirror for seven days.
Ask for help with one thing you have been trying to handle alone: from a parent, a leader, or the Lord.
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: skip the teams. Read Helaman 5:12 together and do the rewriting activity as one group.
Large class: use groups of four for the rewriting activity and hear from only three groups.
Short on time: do the drawing, the Lego story, the rewriting activity, and the final choice.

children.title: Heavenly Father Has a Plan for Me
children.big_idea: Heavenly Father loves me and has a plan for me, and I can trust Him and ask Jesus to help me.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that Heavenly Father loves them and has a plan for them, and will choose one way to follow His plan this week.
prepare: Read paragraphs 25–27 and 36–46 of Sister Runia's talk.
Bring a small set of building blocks (or paper cups to stack).
Bring paper and crayons for each child.
Practice the short truth the children will repeat: Heavenly Father loves me. I can trust His plan.

segments.name: Welcome and song
steps: Greet each child by name. Invite a child to pray.
Sing I Will Follow God's Plan together, or say the title together three times with a clap on each word.
Teach the short truth with actions: Heavenly Father loves me (hug yourself). I can trust His plan (hold hands open like a book). Say it twice.
questions: What do you like to build?

segments.name: Follow the instructions
steps: Set the blocks in the middle. Tell the children you have a plan, and they will build it one step at a time without knowing what it is.

Give one step to each child in turn: Put two blocks side by side with a space between them. Put one long block across the top. Put one block on each end. Put one block in the very middle on top. (Any simple bridge or tower works.)
Ask what they built. Point out that they followed each step even though they could not see the end.

Tell the story: Sister Runia told about her grandson Jaac. When he was seven, he shared a Primary talk. He said he loves Lego bricks and follows the instructions, and that Heavenly Father has a plan like that. Read Jaac's words (first key quote).
Jaac's mother asked what he would do if he did not have the picture on the box, only the instructions. Read his answer: “Yes, because you can trust the one who designed it, and it always turns out.”
questions: Who made the plan for us?
Why can we trust Heavenly Father?

segments.name: Builder says
steps: Have everyone stand. Play Builder Says, like Simon Says, but no one is ever out. Say: Builder says stand tall like a tower. Builder says stretch wide like a bridge. Builder says be small like one little brick. Builder says march in place.
Let one or two children take a turn as the builder.
Sit down and say the short truth together with the actions.
questions: How did you know what to do in the game?

segments.name: Asking for help
steps: Give each child paper and a crayon. Ask them to close their eyes and try to draw a star. Let them look and laugh together at how hard it was.

Tell the story: Sister Runia's brother Kent was in a class where he had to make a statue of his own face out of clay. He could not make the eyes look right. He tried and tried by himself. At last he asked his teacher for help. The teacher was very good. He carved the clay, and soon the eyes looked real. Kent could not have done it alone.
Say: If you would like help with your star, ask me. When a child asks, draw a star in light dots on their paper for them to trace.
Explain that Jesus is like the master teacher. He loves us and wants to help us become like Him. We ask for His help when we pray.
Read the third key quote (paragraph 18) and explain shaping: Heavenly Father is helping us become our very best.
questions: How did it feel when you had help?
How do we ask Heavenly Father and Jesus for help?

segments.name: Standing on the rock
steps: Have the children stand on one foot and wobble. Then have them plant both feet and stand strong.
Explain that everyone has rainy, stormy days. Sister Runia taught that the gospel of Jesus Christ is like a solid rock we stand on in the storm.
Read Helaman 5:12 aloud from the scriptures, or have an older child read it. Ask the children to put a fist on top of a flat hand every time they hear the word rock.

Make a storm together: tap fingers on knees for rain, sway for wind, pat louder for a big storm. When you say Jesus is my rock, everyone plants both feet and stands still and strong. Do it three times.
questions: Who is our rock?

segments.name: Draw and choose
steps: On the back of their paper, invite each child to draw one thing they will do this week to follow Heavenly Father's plan: pray, be kind to someone, help at home, or listen to a scripture story.
Let each child who wishes show the picture and say what they will do. Thank each one.
Check for understanding: ask the children to say the short truth with the actions one more time without your help.
Sing My Heavenly Father Loves Me or I Will Follow God's Plan.
Bear a simple testimony that Heavenly Father loves each child and that Jesus helps us. Tell the children you will ask next week what they did, and close with prayer.

key_quotes.text: I love Lego bricks, and when I get a new box, I open it up and lay out all the pieces and follow the instructions. Just like our Heavenly Father has a plan, and if we follow, it will guide us, and we can build hard things.
Yes, because you can trust the one who designed it, and it always turns out.
God is shaping us into something only He knows we can become.

scriptures.use: Read aloud in the rock segment. Children make a fist on a flat hand each time they hear the word rock.
For older children: one child reads it aloud after the Lego story. Ask what Nephi knew about God even when he did not know everything.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Fale
aligned_quotes.text: I am a child of God and He loves me.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Chibota
aligned_quotes.text: He sees not only who we are but who we can become.

takeaways: Heavenly Father loves me and has a plan for me.
I can trust Heavenly Father even when I cannot see the whole picture.
Jesus helps me when I ask.
act: Say a prayer each day and ask Heavenly Father to help you with one hard thing.
Do the thing you drew to follow Heavenly Father's plan.
Teach your family the short truth and the actions: Heavenly Father loves me. I can trust His plan.

adapt.younger: Ages 3–7: build the blocks yourself with one child helper per step, tell each story in three or four sentences, and repeat the short truth with actions after every segment. Do the storm game twice as long and skip the drawing with eyes closed if it frustrates anyone; go straight to tracing the dotted star. Use Elder Fale's words (aligned quote) as a second line to repeat.
adapt.older: Ages 8–11: let a child give the building steps and another lead Builder Says. Have children read Helaman 5:12 and 1 Nephi 11:17 aloud. Ask a harder question: How can we trust Heavenly Father's plan on a day when things go wrong? Read President Chibota's words (aligned quote) and ask what Heavenly Father might see in them.
